name: Amazon DynamoDB
summary: AWS’s serverless key-value and document database, with single-digit-millisecond reads at any size.
intro: A DynamoDB table has no servers or versions for you to manage. Each item has a partition key, and optionally a sort key. DynamoDB hashes the partition key to decide which storage partition holds the item, and keeps items with the same partition key together, ordered by sort key. So “all orders for customer 1042 in October” is one `Query` that reads a contiguous range. Data is copied across three Availability Zones, and tables have no practical size limit.

Capacity is billed one of two ways. On-demand charges per request, so a table with no traffic pays nothing for throughput. Provisioned charges for a set number of reads and writes per second, with optional auto scaling. Secondary indexes give extra access paths. Transactions update up to 100 items atomically. DynamoDB Streams records every item change in order, which is how Lambda functions react to writes. Global tables replicate a table to several Regions, each accepting writes, with a 99.999% availability SLA.
strengths: Fully serverless: no instances, patches or maintenance windows, and on-demand tables pay no throughput charges when idle
Consistent single-digit-millisecond latency at any table size
Streams and Lambda triggers make event-driven designs straightforward
Multi-Region, multi-active global tables and point-in-time recovery for the last 35 days
limits: No joins or ad-hoc queries: you design keys and indexes around known access patterns
Items are at most 400 KB, and each `Query` or `Scan` call returns at most 1 MB
A transaction covers at most 100 items and 4 MB, and isn’t atomic across Regions in a global table
AWS-only, with its own API; moving off it means rewriting the data layer

story: During the 2004 holiday shopping season, Amazon.com suffered outages that its engineers traced back to commercial databases being pushed past their limits. Many of Amazon’s services, such as the shopping cart, only ever looked data up by primary key, so a full relational database was more than they needed and limited how far they could scale. Amazon built Dynamo, an internal key-value store that spread data across many machines and kept accepting writes even when disks failed or networks split, and described it in a 2007 paper.

Dynamo worked, but few teams wanted to run it. It did nothing to reduce the operational complexity of running large database systems, and engineers didn’t want to become experts in its moving parts across several data centers. Meanwhile AWS’s managed SimpleDB showed that developers preferred simplicity to fine-grained control, although it was limited in size and its performance was hard to predict. DynamoDB, launched on January 18, 2012, set out to combine the two: Dynamo’s incremental scalability and predictable performance, with SimpleDB’s hands-off administration and richer table model.

It now runs much of Amazon itself. On Prime Day 2021, DynamoDB served trillions of API calls, peaking at 89.2 million requests per second. Later additions such as Streams, transactions, on-demand billing and multi-Region tables filled in much of what the first version left out.

choices.choice: A managed service, not software you install
choices.why: Dynamo showed that good technology goes unused if every team has to operate it. SimpleDB showed developers would trade fine-grained control for not running anything.

choices.choice: Partition keys instead of joins and ad-hoc queries
choices.why: Most Amazon services fetched data by key. Hashing that key to spread items across partitions lets a table grow by adding partitions, which a relational design couldn’t do as easily.

Customers declared the reads and writes per second a table needed and DynamoDB reserved that capacity on SSDs, so latency stayed predictable and the price was clear up front. On-demand billing came later, in 2018, for spiky workloads.

timeline.text: Amazon’s Dynamo paper describes its internal key-value store
Streams, Lambda triggers and cross-Region replication become generally available

Global tables gain multi-Region strong consistency
